selection: Best validation checkpoint by average MCC across 14 elements.
metric_scope: Per-nucleotide predictions pooled across test sequences separately for each genomic element. MCC and auPRC are separate metrics, not cross-element or cross-table pooled comparisons.

method_sections_verbatim.Sec16: Model training and evaluationWe train our model using Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 5 × 10−5. We use a batch size of 256 and trained the SegmentNT-3kb model for 10.24 billion tokens, meaning a total of 20.48 million sequences seen during training. The training was done on a cluster of 8 GPU H100 over 20 h. The 10-, 20- and 30-kb models were initialized from the best checkpoint of the respective smaller model for faster adaptation to longer lengths. For example, SegmentNT-30kb model was initialized with the best SegmentNT-20kb checkpoint and fine-tuned for an additional 2.56 billion tokens (0.51 million sequences). We use focal loss33 with γ = 2, which helps the model to focus on ‘harder’ samples, ie the sparse nucleotides that belong to an element.We split our dataset between train, validation and test sets by chromosome. Namely, chromosomes 20 and 21 are used for test, chromosome 22 is used for validation, and the remaining are used for training. We excluded from the test set chunks that contain genes with homology to genes in the train or validation chromosomes, using the annotations from Ensembl BioMart (accessed 8 May 2024). We note that this does not remove homologous distal regulatory elements which could still be inflating performance on these regions. During training, sequences are randomly sampled in the genome with associated annotations. We keep the sequences in the validation and test sets fixed by using a sliding window of length N over the respective chromosomes. The validation set was used to monitor training and for early stopping while the test set was used to evaluate model performance. We sampled the test set ten times to obtain estimates of confidence, each time starting the sliding windows at a different genomic starting position. We used MCC as a validation metric and selected the best checkpoint on the basis of the average score across all 14 genomic elements. During evaluation and testing, we predict 14 probabilities for each nucleotide in a sequence, corresponding to the different element types. We combine these predictions across all sequences into a single array for each element type and calculate performance metrics on the basis of the predictions for every nucleotide across the dataset. These metrics treat each nucleotide as a separate prediction and include the MCC, auPRC, Jaccard similarity and the F1-score.We have also incorporated a region-level metric, the SOV, developed for measuring performance of predictions at the regions-level on 1D sequences in bioinformatics38. Specifically, we used the perl code from http://dna.cs.miami.edu/SOV/ and the default lambda value of 1.0 as recommended in the publication. We tried various values of this parameter and observed minor variations in the results.
method_sections_verbatim.Sec17: Model ablations and baselinesSegmentNT is made of a DNA encoder (NT-Multispecies-v2 (500M)) and a 1D U-Net segmentation head, as described above. To evaluate the added value of using a pretrained backbone encoder, we performed different model ablations and compared it on the 3 kb dataset with the following models. (1) The SegmentNT where we use the NT v1 2.5B 1000G model22 as backbone (this is the only model in this study where the backbone is not the NT-Multispecies-v2 (500M)), featuring 2.6 billion parameters including the segmentation head. (2) The SegmentNT-3kb model (563M), initialized with the NT-Multispecies-v2 weights but where we only fine-tune the segmentation head. (3) Two versions of the SegmentNT model (563M) whose encoder is initialized with random weights, where we train either all parameters or only the segmentation head. (4) Two versions of the U-Net segmentation head alone, with 63 million and 252 million parameters respectively, which take one-hot encoded DNA sequences as input instead of the embeddings outputted by the DNA encoder. (5) The same segmentation head where we first pass the one-hot representation in a linear layer, which adds 3 million parameters, bringing the model to 66 million parameters, to upscale it to the embedding dimension before passing in the U-Net (1,024 embedding).We compared SegmentNT with the two state-of-the-art single-nucleotide model architectures BPNet39 and SpliceAI40 on the 3-kb dataset, using directly one-hot encoded DNA sequences (of L = 3,000) and varying their embedding size to test different model scaling. We trained two randomly initialized versions of the BPNet model with embedding sizes of 64 (original model) and 1,024, bringing the number of parameters to respectively 120,000 and 29 million. In addition, we trained three randomly initialized versions of the SpliceAI model with an embedding size of 32 to match the original model (700,000 parameters) and embedding sizes of 256 (44 million) and 920 (573 million) to upscale the model.As with the SegmentNT models, we monitored the training by validating on sequences from chromosome 22 and selected the best checkpoint on the basis of the highest average MCC score across the 14 types of element (see Supplementary Table 1 for the number of sequences seen during training for all models). We present all model results in Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3.
